title: Answer every interested reply within the hour
summary: Find replies that show interest, draft an answer that books the call, and send it once you approve.
description: An interested reply goes cold fast. Answering within the hour books far more meetings than answering the next day, but replies land across many mailboxes and sequencers. This playbook reads the inbox, picks out the replies that ask a question or show interest, drafts a short answer that moves to a meeting, and waits for you to approve each one.

connections.label: An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

steps.say: List replies from the last day that nobody has answered yet.
Read each conversation and keep the ones that are interested or ask a question.
Tag them so the team sees them.
Draft a short reply in the same thread that answers the question and offers the booking link.

guardrails: Every reply waits for a person to approve it before it is sent.
Out-of-office, unsubscribe and not-interested replies are left alone.

measure.how: Median minutes from an interested reply to our answer.
Share of interested replies that become a booked meeting.

prompt: Run the "Answer interested replies" playbook. Go through replies from the last 24 hours that nobody has answered. Keep the ones that show interest or ask a question, and tag them "Interested". For each one, draft a short, friendly answer in the same thread that answers their question and offers a time to talk with {{booking_link}}. Leave out-of-office, unsubscribe and not-interested replies alone. Hold every reply for my approval.
example: Of 140 replies one morning, 9 were interested. Each got a three-line answer drafted with the booking link; the team approved them in a few minutes and 4 booked a call the same day.

title: Fix your SEO quick wins
summary: Crawl your site, find the issues that cost the most clicks, and turn each one into a fix your team or coding agent can ship.
description: Most sites have a handful of problems that cost far more than the rest: pages that rank on page two for searches with real volume, broken pages that still get links, missing titles on pages people do find. This playbook crawls the site, reads Search Console, and ranks the fixes by the clicks they are likely to bring.

steps.say: Find the site and crawl it.
Read what the audit found and how the site does in search.
Rank the fixes by the clicks they are likely to bring and keep the top ten.
Turn each one into a prompt a coding agent can work from.

guardrails: Never changes the site itself; fixes go to the fixes list for a person or a coding agent.

measure.how: Search Console clicks to the fixed pages, 28 days before and after.

prompt: Run the "SEO quick wins" playbook for {{site}}. Crawl the site, read what the audit found and how its pages do in Google Search Console, and rank the problems by how many clicks fixing them is likely to bring. Give me the top ten as fixes, each with a prompt I can hand to a coding agent.
example: For northpeak.example the top fix was a pricing page ranking 11th for a search with 2,400 monthly impressions and no meta description; the second was a broken docs page that still had 14 links pointing at it.

title: Tag every link you share
summary: Find the traffic you can't credit to a channel and give every link you share a campaign tag.
description: When links go out without tags, visits and sign-ups land in "direct" or "unknown" and nobody can tell which channel worked. This playbook looks at where your site's visits come from, finds the channels with untagged traffic, and makes tagged campaign links for each one, using one spelling for every source.

connections.label: Your web analytics, to compare with what Outflare sees

steps.say: Read the channels and sources campaign links can use.
Compare where visits come from with the campaigns that exist, and list the channels with untagged traffic.
Create a campaign for each gap and a tagged link for every place the brand shares links.

guardrails: Only creates campaigns and links; it never changes your site or posts anything.

measure.how: Share of visits with a known channel and campaign, before and after.

prompt: Run the "Tag every link" playbook for {{brand}}. Look at where the site's visits come from and which campaigns already exist, and tell me which channels send traffic we can't credit. Then create a campaign for each gap and a tagged link for every place we share links (newsletter, social profiles, partner pages, email signatures), and give me the list.
example: Northpeak found that 31% of sign-ups came from "unknown". Most were from the newsletter and two partner blogs; three campaigns and eight links fixed it the same week.

title: Welcome new sign-ups and get them to their first win
summary: A short welcome journey that follows what each new user does, not how many days have passed.
description: Most welcome emails go out on a timer: day 1, day 3, day 7. People who already got going get told how to start, and people who are stuck get nothing useful. This playbook finds the one action that tells you a new user got value (their first API call, first project, first purchase), then builds a journey that stops as soon as they take it and nudges them with a specific next step until they do.

data.label: Sign-up and product events sent to Outflare

connections.label: An email provider for lifecycle email
An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: first_win
inputs.label: What a first win looks like
inputs.help: The action that shows a new user got value. Leave it empty and the agent suggests one from your events.

steps.say: Read the brand's context so the emails sound like the brand.
Look at the events new users send in their first week and pick the one that best marks a first win, unless one was given.
Write three short emails (welcome, a nudge with one concrete next step, and a last helpful tip) as templates.
Build a journey that starts on sign-up, sends the emails, and exits as soon as the first-win event arrives.
Ask a person to turn the journey on.

guardrails: Only people who signed up themselves get these emails, and the contact rules and opt-outs apply to every send.
The journey is turned on only after a person approves it.

measure.how: Share of new sign-ups who reach the first win within 7 days, before and after.
Median hours from sign-up to the first-win event.

prompt: Run the "Welcome new sign-ups" playbook for {{brand}}. Look at the events new users send in their first week and find the action that best shows they got value (use "{{first_win}}" if I gave one). Then write three short, plain emails in our voice: a welcome, a nudge with one concrete next step, and a final tip. Build a lifecycle journey that starts on sign-up, sends them over the first week, and stops as soon as someone reaches that first win. Don't turn the journey on: show me the emails and the journey first.
example: Northpeak's events showed that users who create a project in their first day stay three times longer. The journey sends a welcome straight away, "Create your first project in two minutes" after a day, and a template gallery link after three days, and leaves anyone who already created one.

title: Get named in AI answers
summary: See which questions AI assistants answer without naming you, and what to publish so they do.
description: People ask ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity which tool to use. If the answer names three competitors and not you, you lose the sale before anyone visits your site. This playbook samples the questions buyers ask in your category, finds the ones where competitors are named and you aren't, reads the pages the assistants cite, and lists what to publish or correct.

connections.label: An AI model to ask the questions

inputs.name: category
inputs.label: What you sell, in a few words
inputs.example: project planning software for small agencies

steps.say: Read how often AI answers name the brand today.
Add a set of buyer questions for the category if there isn't one.
Read the answers where competitors are named and the brand isn't, and the pages they cite.
Compare with what competitors publish.
Post a short list of pages to write or facts to correct.

guardrails: Questions are asked with the workspace's own AI key, within its monthly AI limit.

measure.how: Share of sampled answers that name the brand, before and after.

prompt: Run the "Get named in AI answers" playbook for {{brand}}, which sells {{category}}. Check how often AI assistants name us today. If there's no set of buyer questions for our category, add one. Then find the answers that name competitors but not us, read the pages they cite, and give me a short list of pages to write or facts to correct so we get named.
example: Northpeak was named in 4 of 40 answers about agency project tools. Most answers cited two comparison pages and a review site, none of which listed Northpeak; the list started with asking those three to add it.

title: Write content from your customers' questions
summary: Turn the questions people ask in replies into briefs for pages that answer them in search.
description: The questions prospects and customers ask by email are the same ones others type into search and AI assistants. This playbook collects them from the inbox, groups the ones that come up again and again, checks whether the site already answers them, and writes a short brief for each page that's missing.

connections.label: An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: days
inputs.label: How far back to look, in days

steps.say: Read replies from the period and pull out every question.
Group questions that mean the same thing and count them.
Check which ones the site already answers and which pages target them.
Write a brief for each missing page and post them to the mission.

guardrails: Briefs never quote a customer by name or include their email address or company.

measure.how: Search Console clicks to pages written from the briefs.
How often the same questions arrive by email, before and after.

prompt: Run the "Content from customer questions" playbook. Read the replies from the last {{days}} days and pull out every question people ask about our product or problem. Group the ones that mean the same thing and count them. Check which ones our site already answers, then write a short brief for a page that answers each of the top five that it doesn't. Never quote anyone by name or include their email address or company.
example: Northpeak's inbox asked "can I export to CSV?" 23 times in 90 days and the site had no page about it. The brief became a docs page that now ranks first for "northpeak csv export".
